en.title: Forgotten Island Explores Girlhood Through Vibrant Filipino Mythology
en.summary: DreamWorks Animation's latest, Forgotten Island, dives deep into the enduring bonds of friendship and the magic of animation. It's a visually stunning journey into a world rich with Filipino culture.
en.body:
DreamWorks Animation has long been a beacon of imaginative storytelling, consistently delivering films that resonate with audiences of all ages. From the early days with **Antz** and **The Prince of Egypt** to modern triumphs like **How to Train Your Dragon** and **The Wild Robot**, the studio has cultivated a reputation for crafting heartfelt and visually spectacular narratives. Their latest offering, **Forgotten Island**, continues this tradition, presenting a vibrant tapestry woven with themes of girlhood, friendship, and the boundless potential of animation itself.

The film centers on **Jo** (voiced by **H.E.R.**) and **Raissa** (voiced by **Liza Soberano**), two childhood best friends whose lives are intertwined with the mythical island of Nakali, a place whispered about in stories passed down by Jo’s grandmother, Lola. While their youthful dreams of visiting Nakali seem destined to fade with time and diverging paths—Raissa’s impending departure for college in America looms—fate intervenes on their final night together. They find themselves transported to Nakali, a realm brimming with the magical creatures and rich folklore of Filipino mythology. Directed by **Januel Mercado** and **Joel Crawford**, **Forgotten Island** promises a colorful exploration of these themes, leaning heavily into its cultural roots.

## A Celebration of Friendship and Culture

**Forgotten Island** is more than just an animated adventure; it's a profound rumination on the complexities of female friendship and the enduring power of shared memories. The narrative beautifully captures the bittersweet transition from childhood camaraderie to the divergent paths adulthood often forces upon us. The film’s dedication to showcasing Filipino mythology and culture is a significant aspect, offering audiences a chance to immerse themselves in a world less frequently explored in mainstream animation. This cultural richness, combined with the universal themes of friendship and growing up, creates a compelling experience that speaks to both devoted fans of Filipino heritage and newcomers alike. The early buzz suggests a film that is both visually dazzling and emotionally resonant, a true testament to the directors' vision.

## What Fans Can Expect

The anticipation for **Forgotten Island** is palpable, especially among fans eager to see DreamWorks Animation continue its streak of original storytelling. The film’s emphasis on cultural representation and its exploration of relatable coming-of-age themes are expected to strike a chord with a broad audience. The voice cast, featuring talents like **H.E.R.**, **Liza Soberano**, **Dave Franco**, and **Lea Salonga**, further amplifies the excitement, promising nuanced performances that bring these characters and their relationships to life. Early reactions highlight the film’s vibrant animation and its heartfelt narrative, positioning it as a must-watch for animation enthusiasts and anyone who cherishes stories about the bonds of friendship.

## What's Next

Following its theatrical run, **Forgotten Island** is slated for a digital and VOD release in October 2026, with DVD and Blu-ray editions expected in November 2026. Fans can look forward to experiencing this celebration of friendship and culture from the comfort of their homes.

(They are very different films, with the latter being a loose adaptation of Seven Samurai and the former being… a Woody Allen movie with ants. It’s still weird.) The studio has consistently created some of the best animated films on this side of the globe, from early stunners like The Prince of Egypt and The Road to El Dorado , to staples like Shrek and How to Train Your Dragon , and their most recent tour de force The Wild Robot . While Pixar has been eaten by Disney and sentenced to manufacturing sequels of their earlier hits, and Illumination Studios spends most of their time saturating the world with yellow minions, DreamWorks Animation remains one of the more sizable studios that has largely stuck to its brief of making imaginative and affecting stories for kids and families. Forgotten Island is the latest worthy addition to that crew, and I hope that more people head to the theater to enjoy it. The reason why is nothing so surprising— Forgotten Island is focused on a piece of childhood that rarely gets enough attention in the animated sphere or films in general: the wilds of girlhood and female friendship. It’s also set in the Philippines and focused on Filippino mythology in order to create the eponymous island our heroes travel to, and these two factors alone will cause a certain contingent of the online sphere to label it “woke” and ignore it.
